candidates.text:
I would strongly consider uninstalling any third party js right now if I were you. Especially if it comes from a startup.

Analytics, monitoring, etc are all massive site takeover risks. If you use a tracking script from a third party SaaS, then if they get hacked the hackers have total control over your site too.

This is what took down Polymarket today. They used a tiny script from a SaaS that tracks page load speed. That company got hacked, and the hackers subsequently stole millions from Polymarket users.

If you want to use analytics safely, I would use a product that lets you pin the tracking script and control when it changes. Most of the mature products support this, e.g. Sentry, Amplitude, PostHog, Mixpanel, Heap. If not, you need to trust the company behind it a lot...

Railway got hacked last week. Railway! That's a very competent team, with particularly strong infra chops. The agent swarms are on another level.

A typical analytics company is nowhere near as sophisticated. You should ask yourself: do I trust this company's security more than Railway? I was an analytics CTO in a past life, and I will be the first to admit: we had some great people but we were not on this level.

We (Detail) just uninstalled our session replay, which was a product I loved but is not worth the risk right now.

I hate to write this because I spent a good chunk of my 20s benefitting from product teams taking a chance on a nothing startup and installing our js on their site. But in the past two weeks this risk vector has exploded. It's better for the ecosystem if we move away from third party js as fast as we can.

candidates.text:
How to get ppl to read your stuff:

People ask to review their blog posts and my response is usually some polite form of "it doesn't matter, no one will read it." It's a rough thing, but it's true. John Grisham in a 2017 interview said he's irritated by new authors debuting 1000 page novels because they haven't earned the right to publish books that long. That was 2017 and this is now and you haven't earned so much as a right to publish a screen-long blog post

Scott Alexander can do it because he wrote interesting stuff for many years. Pg can do it because he wrote useful stuff. Dario Amodei can do it because he built probably the most important technology in history of the world. But you didn't do any of these things (btw be honest did *you* read every word in machines of loving grace from start to finish?)

If you're new you have a baseline right to 15 tokens of ppl's attention. If these are really good tokens, you've earned the right to another 50. And if those are really *really* good, you've got another 50, and so on. See, every 50 tokens an interrupt fires in ppl's brains and they decide from scratch whether to keep reading or switch to literally anything else on the internet

So don't worry about spelling, grammar, structure, thesis, capitalization, punctuation, or any of that writing stuff because it doesn't matter. You must produce valuable tokens, 15 first, then 50 tokens at a time. Self-review for that, you'll know in your gut if you're doing it. Attention is all you need

Btw openai tokenizer tells me this post is 9 -> 95 -> 76 -> 84 -> 65 -> 42. So i'm breaking my own rules a bit, i need to get better

candidates.text:
Procrastination.

We've all been there. There's that thing you need to get done.

It's nagging at you.
It's important that you do it.

But for some reason... you just don't?

You know you should do it. You know you'll feel better once you've done it. But instead, you find literally ANYTHING else to do.

And the whole time you're doing those other things, you have that little voice reminding you of what you're avoiding.

So you don't even get to properly enjoy fucking around...

Wonderful.

STOP.

Wouldn't you rather not be a retard instead?

Here's how.

And this is something you need to be vigilant about, and PRACTICE until it becomes an automatic habit.

The very next time you catch yourself in the act of procrastinating...

INTERRUPT IT.

Say out loud, or firmly in your mind:

“This is bullshit. Let me get on task. I'm going to go do [THE THING YOU WERE AVOIDING] right. fucking. now.”

And as you say it, MOVE YOUR BODY toward that thing.

Physically interrupt your procrastination by GETTING UP and MOVING YOUR LEGS toward whatever you need to be doing.

Give yourself an instruction, and immediately FOLLOW IT.

Before you finish the video.
Before you check another notification.
Before you negotiate yourself into “just another 5 minutes.”
UP. MOVE.
And yes, if you're procrastinating digitally, scrolling bullshit on your phone or disappearing down some rabbit hole on your laptop, the same thing applies.

Put your phone down. Get up from your desk. Walk a few strides.

“This is bullshit. Let me get on task. I'm going to finish that proposal. Right. Fucking. Now.”

Then sit back down, open the [proposal, for example], and WRITE THE NEXT SENTENCE.

That last part matters.

Follow the interruption with an ACTUAL piece of the thing you've been avoiding.

Make the call. Write the sentence. Put your shoes on and walk out the door.

Something concrete. Something you can DO immediately.

This can feel like magic because you've physically interrupted the exact behaviour that was keeping you occupied, and given yourself a clear instruction to act on.

Think about what usually happens when you catch yourself procrastinating.

You notice.
You feel a little guilty.
You tell yourself you should stop.

And then your thumb scrolls again.

The awareness was there. You knew EXACTLY what you were doing.
You just carried on doing it.
This is where you intervene.

The moment you NOTICE becomes the moment you MOVE.

And every time you catch yourself drifting again, practice the same response.

Catch it. Interrupt it. Get back on task.

No need to spend the next twenty minutes conducting an investigation into why you're such a fucking disappointment.

Nothing is actually wrong with you, it's just that these apps and sites are designed by people who's full time job it is to capture as much of your screen-time as physically possible, and they succeeded in making you go "Oooh shinyyyy"

Ok. So. You've already spent enough time avoiding the work...

Use that moment of awareness while you have it.

Practice until “I'm procrastinating” becomes your cue to physically redirect yourself, and your body is already moving before you've finished manufacturing the next excuse.

You can begin while you still don't feel like it.

I would go as far to suggest that you DELETE "I need to feel like doing something, in order to do it." from your mind, as soon as possible.

Because the moment you do, is the moment you have unlocked an intense degree of freedom and personal sovereignty. 

No longer are you at the mercy of needing to feel a certain way. No longer are you at the mercy of needing perfect conditions to perform.

Fuck that off.

Now.

There's probably something you've been thinking about the entire time you've been reading this.

Something you know you need to do.

Get up.

Right. Fucking. Now.

candidates.text:
Once agents write most of the code, the eval suite is the reviewer.

Most teams still run it like a test suite. Every case, on every change, then wait for a green check.

What I wold do instead:

1. Split evals into a gate set and an audit set
The gate runs on every prompt, tool or harness change and stays small. The audit runs nightly on everything.

2. Tag every eval with the prompts, tools and code paths it touches
A change then only runs its own slice and not the whole suite.

3. Promote from traces, not from guesses
A nightly job reads the failed traces and moves the cases that actually caught regressions into the gate.

On the eval system I built at the neolab, this took a full run from 30 mins to 5.

The gate should get smaller and meaner over time, not bigger.

candidates.text:
there's a tiny subset of people who take a redpill and *experience relief*

(btw this is actually a tweet about friendship)

bad/dark news about the nature of reality is *relaxing* to them so long as it helps make their reality model increasingly *consistent* and feels *true* even if it is terrifying or ugly. as opposed to the self-deception and cognitive dissonance embraced by those who prefer the bluepill and favour clean, legible reality models.

yes, aspect x of reality is totally fucked up -  say they read 48 laws of power or watched gangs of wasseypur or read a vgr essay or maybe something even subtler that they saw or experienced. but the consequent updates to their reality model show that it is fucked up in a coherent manner. what seemed to be chaos before suddenly settles into some semblance of cause and effect for them, fucked up though that cause/effect may be, and this is *anxiety-reducing* for them. it means they know what they can and can't do about it. they can reason about their dharma. and their karma.

these are the friends worth making.

not all, mind you. defectors abound among redpillers. comes with the territory. but the cooperators, oh my. they will change the trajectory of your life. 

probably also worth noting tangentially, that by and large, redpill cooperators run in groups usually implicit and informal, but not always. open source is FULL of such groups of both kinds, for obvious reasons. (interestingly they don't have to like each other, in fact often i've observed that in most cases folks are barely able to tolerate one another, but that doesn't preclude consistent cooperation - as a beloved friend pithily puts it तू तो साला लुंड है, पर लुंड तो मेरा ही है। just go read any of linus torvalds famous emails on oss mailing lists. extreme cooperation often looks like that.)

bluepillers do not (cannot) really grasp things like love and loss and loyalty, and *cannot be reliably cooperated with*. they tend to be moviebrained about these things 
and those among them who are cooperation-biased will defect on others for reasons that are totally random but feel true and consistent to that person. you will see these lost souls everywhere "I'm such a nice person but..." and they are such nice people...

but not great friend material, basically.

candidates.text:
I think @julianweisser's reply under this pins down the exact moment it happens. Most investors end the meeting with "we'll follow up," and that sentence is where the ghost gets made. A no to someone's face is expensive. "We'll follow up" costs nothing in the room and sounds kind, so the no gets postponed. Then the 20 to 50 pitches you're describing land on top of it, and the postponed no never gets written. So you're both right: it starts as politeness, and busyness finishes it.

I see a lot of this from the middle, because plenty of no's come to me instead of to the founder. The fix I've landed on is price, not courage. When a meeting I'm arranging goes quiet, I don't send "any update?" I ask whether it's still a priority and say there's no pressure, I can find the founder someone else. That makes no the easiest possible reply, so it actually gets sent. "Any update?" asks for an awkward sentence, so it sits there.

I was reading about how marriages got arranged in 1930s Kona, Hawaii, and it's the best picture I've found of what "knowing how the system works" means. A Japanese go-between would bring a young man to a family's house on the pretense of buying chickens or pigs. The girl's mother served tea, and she always turned down the first proposal, saying her daughter was needed at home. Saying yes at the first call would have lowered the family's dignity, and everyone at that table knew the refusal wasn't the real answer. The code worked because the whole room could read it.

Venture has plenty of code ("keep us posted," "not a fit right now"), but only one side of the table was taught it. Founders with a network hear a no. Founders without one read it literally and wait for weeks. Those are the founders I most want to find, and translating for them is part of what a go-between owes.
